newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan govt panel to suggest scrapping Monju--paper.
newsitem.headline: Japan govt panel to suggest scrapping Monju--paper.

text.p: A government panel is to suggest Japan consider abolishing Monju, a trouble-ridden prototype fast-breeder nuclear reactor, a business daily reported on Wednesday.

The Nihon Keizai Shimbun said the panel on financial reforms plans to suggest the step in view of mounting criticism of Japan's nuclear policy following a series of accidents at nuclear plants and nuclear waste recycling facilities.
Government officials could not be immediately reached for comment.
The paper said the panel would call for drastically scaling down the project if it could not be scrapped.
The panel wants to streamline large-scale projects which require massive public funding, it said.
In December 1995, an estimated two to three tonnes of liquid sodium leaked from a cooling system in Monju, a 280,000 kilowatt (kw) reactor located on the Sea of Japan coast in Fukui Prefecture.
The step forced the manual shutting down of the reactor, operated by the state-run Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corp (PNC).
Monju -- which burns plutonium refined from spent fuel from conventional reactors -- has not resumed operations since the accident, and no timetable has been announced for a possible resumption.

The accident at Monju greatly undermined the public confidence in the nation's nuclear policy. Subsequent revelations of attempts to cover up the scale of the accident by the PNC further tarnished the industry's image.

In March, a PNC-run nuclear fuel reprocessing plant in Tokaimura on the Pacific coast was the scene of Japan's worst-ever nuclear accident when an explosion exposed some 37 workers to low levels of radiation.
Because fast-breeder nuclear reactors produce more fuel than they consume, the Monju programme was seen as the cornerstone of resource-poor Japan's nuclear power policy.
Monju's scrapping could force the authorities to drastically review the nation's energy policy.
The newspaper said scrapping Monju would save the nation at least an average 20 billion yen a year, which is the cost of the reactor's maintenance and checks even when it is not operating.
